parts.article:
The Animal Connection
 
Professor of anthropology Pat Shipman looks at the ways in which our relationships with animals have shaped our own human evolution.
 
(A) Travel anywhere and you see something so common it may not even catch your attention. Wherever there are people, animals are being walked, herded and fed. Many, such as dogs, cats and sheep, are domesticated, but you will also find people living alongside wild creatures like monkeys and wolves. Close contact with animals is not confined to one particular culture, region or ethnic group but is a universal human trait.
 
(B) On the face of it this makes little sense. No other mammal adopts individuals from another species, with good reason. Since the ultimate prize in evolution is perpetuating your genes, providing food for another species is counterproductive to success. Even if pets offer friendship, that cannot explain why our bond with other species arose in the first place. Who would bring a ferocious wolf into their home in the hope that thousands of years later it would become a loving pet?
 
(C) As an anthropologist I have tried to understand this puzzle by looking to the past for the origins of our link with animals. What I found was a long and unbroken evolutionary trail of evidence I call the ‘animal connection’. This trail links to three important developments in human evolution: tool making, language and domestication. If I am correct, and I believe that further research will conclusively show that I am, the animal connection is a hugely significant force instrumental in our global success.
 
(D) The trail begins at least 2.6 million years ago. That is when the first tools appear in the archaeological record. This development required the intellectual breakthrough of realizing that the properties of an object can be altered. Man learnt how to turn stone into small, sharp items that could cut up animal carcasses, providing them with an evolutionary shortcut to becoming predators.
 
(E) There were many consequences of the new hunting lifestyle. On the plus side, eating more meat and fat was a requirement for the increase in relative brain size. And since meat tends to come in bigger packages than leaves and roots, meat eaters could spend less time finding food and more on activities like learning and social interaction. On the minus side, preying on animals put our ancestors into direct competition with the other predators that shared their ecosystem, animals such as lions and hyenas. To get the upper hand, they needed more than just tools, and that is where the animal connection comes in. What made it possible for our ancestors to compete successfully with true carnivores was the ability to pay very close attention to the habits of both potential prey and competitors. Knowledge was power, so we acquired a deep understanding of the minds of other animals. Another significant consequence of becoming more predatory was the need to live at lower densities, as successful predators soon exhaust food supplies. The record of the geographic distribution of our ancestors provides further support for my idea that the animal connection has shaped our evolution. Early man lived in Africa and nowhere else, but then underwent a dramatic expansion in territory, forced by the search for new hunting grounds.
 
(F) Throughout the period of these enormous changes in the lifestyle of our ancestors, gathering, sharing and recording knowledge became increasingly advantageous, and examples of prehistoric art that appear in Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia allow us to eavesdrop on their conversations. Through the art, we realize the main topic was animals: their colours, shapes, postures and habits. This focus is even more striking considering that scenes of human life are rarely depicted. Pictures of people, social interaction and ceremonies are rare.
 
(G) This leads me on to the development of language. Nobody doubts this proved a major adaptive advantage to our ancestors in developing complex behaviours. How it arose, however, remains a mystery. I believe I am the first to propose a continuity between the strong human-animal link that appeared 2.6 million years ago and the origin of language. The complexity and importance of animal-related information, indicated in the predominance of animal images, spurred early humans to move beyond what other species could achieve. Vervet monkeys, for example, have different cries for eagles and snakes, but they cannot discuss what threats might appear tomorrow. The property of full language is that it is comprised of vocabulary and grammatical rules that can be combined in an infinite number of ways to convey fine shades of meaning.
 
(H) As our ancestors became more involved with animals, the third product of the animal connection appeared: domestication, which has long been linked with the keeping of animals like sheep. Domestic animals are usually considered as ‘walking larders’, or easy food sources, reflecting the idea that the basis of this change was a drive for greater food security. Looking at the origins of domestication for clues to its underlying reasons, I found fundamental flaws in this idea. Instead, my analysis suggests domestication emerged as a natural progression of our close association with, and understanding of, other species. If domestication was about knowing where your next meal was coming from, the first domesticate ought to have been a food source, yet analysis of fossils shows that the domestication of dogs pre-dated that of any other species, even plants, from wolves. Furthermore, if the objective was to have meat to eat, you wouldn’t select an animal that eats two kilograms of meat a day. It was familiarity with this species that led to eventual domestication.

Questions 27–31
Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 27–31 on your answer sheet, write.

Q27 Travellers are more likely to notice wild animals than domesticated ones.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q28 All cultures demonstrate a need to have close contact with animals.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q29 Animals benefit from allowing other animal species to share food resources.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q30 It is unlikely that people initially domesticated wolves for future companionship.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q31 There are periods of human evolution for which we have little information about man’s relationship with animals.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 32–36
Complete the summary using the list of words, A-J, below.
Write the correct letter, A-J, in boxes 32–36 on your answer sheet.
Hunting and the animal connection
Around 2.6 million years ago, humans became predators after they realized the possibility of object . Once humans were hunters, they benefited from better and extra time which could be spent on non-physical activities. However, the more humans came to depend on meat as a food source, the more there was between them and other predators. Humans needed to find an advantage over animals such as lions and hyenas. It wasn’t a spear or knife that gave them this advantage, but the skills that humans began to develop. Then, because humans were such successful predators, they required more and this led to groups of people moving away from Africa.
  • A nutrition
  • B competition
  • C leadership
  • D adaptation
  • E territory
  • F trade
  • G connection
  • H observation
  • I behavior
  • J worship
Questions 37–40
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 37–40 on your answer sheet.

Q37 What is the writer’s main argument in the sixth paragraph?

  • A Prehistoric art allows us to date human migration patterns.
  • B Early man valued the communication of knowledge about animal behaviour and appearance.
  • C There is evidence of big lifestyle differences between early humans in different regions.
  • D There was little spoken interaction between different groups of people.

Q38 What is the writer doing in the seventh paragraph?

  • A rejecting an established theory about human evolution.
  • B emphasizing the value of art in language development.
  • C expressing doubt about the initial purpose of communication.
  • D making a claim about the way that language developed.

Q39 The writer refers to vervet monkeys in order to:

  • A indicate which animal species have a kind of basic language.
  • B show how danger is a significant motivation for human communication.
  • C highlight the sophistication of human communication.
  • D suggest a possible influence on the way early humans interacted.

Q40 The writer says that the ‘walking larder’ idea

  • A fails to explain the purpose of domestication.
  • B is true only for domesticated animals.
  • C supports the idea the writer proposes.
  • D is based on research the writer has carried out.

reference:
Q27

干扰 你可能会觉得野生动物少见所以更吸引眼球，但做判断题绝不能自己脑补，文章没比大小就是 NOT GIVEN 。

句子 Travel anywhere and you see something so common it may not even catch your attention. Wherever there are people, animals are being walked, herded and fed. Many, such as dogs, cats and sheep, are domesticated, but you will also find people living alongside wild creatures like monkeys and wolves. (第1段)

解析 文章第1段确实提到了野生动物（wild creatures）和驯养动物（domesticated），但完全没有比较旅行者“更容易注意到哪一种（more likely to notice）” 。

Q28

解析 原文明确说到，与动物的密切接触不是局限于某个特定文化，而是一种“普遍的人类特征（universal human trait）”，完美等同于题干的“所有文化（All cultures）”都有这种需求 。

干扰 不要看到题干里的“All”就立刻判定为太绝对而选 NO，原文的“universal（普遍的）”刚好稳稳支撑了这个绝对词 。

句子 Close contact with animals is not confined to one particular culture, region or ethnic group but is a universal human trait. (第1段)

Q29

解析 题干说动物允许其他物种共享食物会“受益（benefit）”，但原文明确说给其他物种提供食物对进化成功是“适得其反的（counterproductive）”，两者意思完全相反 。

干扰 你可能不认识 counterproductive 这个词，但只要看到前面说的进化的终极奖赏是延续自己的基因，就能猜出把食物分给别人绝对不是什么好事 。

句子 Since the ultimate prize in evolution is perpetuating your genes, providing food for another species is counterproductive to success. (第2段)

Q30

句子 Who would bring a ferocious wolf into their home in the hope that thousands of years later it would become a loving pet? (第2段)

解析 作者在第2段抛出了一个反问句：“谁会把凶猛的狼带回家，指望它几千年后变成可爱的宠物呢？”，反问的语气代表作者认为这是极不可能的（unlikely），与题干态度完全一致 。

干扰 你可能会觉得反问句没有直接给出判断，但在英文阅读里，这种带修辞的反问就是在强烈表达“一开始绝不可能是为了未来的陪伴”这一观点 。

Q31

解析 题干说人类进化史上有关于人兽关系信息很少的“空白期”，但作者明确表示，他找到的是一条“漫长且没有断裂的（long and unbroken）”证据链 。

干扰 题干的“little information（信息很少）”和原文的“unbroken... evidence（不断裂的证据链）”构成了直接对立，所以不是 NOT GIVEN，而是明确的 NO 。

句子 What I found was a long and unbroken evolutionary trail of evidence I call the 'animal connection'. (第3段)

Q32

解析 原文说人类意识到物体的属性可以被“改变（altered）”，这对应了把石头“改造/适应（adaptation）”成锋利的工具的过程 。

干扰 你可能想选 behavior，但这空填的是对“object（物体）”采取的动作，只有 adaptation 能够完美替换原文的 altered（改变/改造） 。

句子 This development required the intellectual breakthrough of realizing that the properties of an object can be altered. Man learnt how to turn stone into small, sharp items... (第4段)

Q33

解析 原文提到人类吃更多的肉和脂肪，并因此节省了找食物的时间，肉和脂肪带来的直接好处就是更好的“营养（nutrition）” 。

干扰 不要错选 trade（贸易），当时的人类只是在打猎填饱肚子，获取高能量食物，完全没有提到任何商业交换行为 。

句子 On the plus side, eating more meat and fat was a requirement for the increase in relative brain size. And since meat tends to come in bigger packages than leaves and roots, meat eaters could spend less time finding food and more on activities like learning and social interaction. (第5段)

Q34

干扰 这道题定位非常直接，只要找到“other predators”就能立刻看到前方的 competition 这个词，不要去瞎猜别的抽象概念 。

句子 On the minus side, preying on animals put our ancestors into direct competition with the other predators that shared their ecosystem, animals such as lions and hyenas. (第5段)

解析 原文明确写道，捕猎动物让人类的祖先与其他捕食者（如狮子和鬣狗）陷入了直接的“竞争（competition）”中，原词重现，直接填 B 即可 。

Q35

解析 原文强调人类能战胜其他食肉动物的优势在于“密切关注（pay very close attention to）”猎物和竞争者的习性，这正是“观察（observation）”技能的同义替换 。

干扰 你可能会纠结 connection（联系），但这句明确在谈论如何通过了解动物习性来获得上风，靠的是仔细“看”和分析，即观察力 。

句子 What made it possible for our ancestors to compete successfully with true carnivores was the ability to pay very close attention to the habits of both potential prey and competitors. (第5段)

Q36

解析 原文提到因为捕猎成功导致食物消耗快，早期人类被迫寻找新的猎场，经历了一场戏剧性的“领地（territory）”扩张，导致他们离开非洲 。

干扰 只要定位到最后一句“moving away from Africa”，对照原文“lived in Africa... expansion in territory”，就能百分百锁定 E 选项 。

句子 Another significant consequence of becoming more predatory was the need to live at lower densities, as successful predators soon exhaust food supplies. The record of the geographic distribution of our ancestors provides further support for my idea... Early man lived in Africa and nowhere else, but then underwent a dramatic expansion in territory, forced by the search for new hunting grounds. (第5段)

Q37

句子 Throughout the period of these enormous changes in the lifestyle of our ancestors, gathering, sharing and recording knowledge became increasingly advantageous, and examples of prehistoric art... allow us to eavesdrop on their conversations. Through the art, we realize the main topic was animals: their colours, shapes, postures and habits. (第6段)

解析 第6段的核心论点是：早期人类收集和分享知识变得越来越有利，而通过史前艺术我们可以发现，他们交流的“主要话题（main topic）”就是动物的颜色、姿态和习性 。

干扰 A 选项错在“给迁徙定年”，C 选项错在“生活方式差异”，D 选项错在“很少口头交流”（原文说的是艺术让我们“偷听到他们的对话”，暗示交流很丰富） 。

Q38

解析 在第7段中，作者明确提出了一个新主张（propose）：把260万年前出现的人兽联系与“语言的起源（origin of language）”建立了一种连续性 。

干扰 作者并不是在“推翻既定理论”（排除 A），也没有再强调艺术（排除 B），更没有怀疑沟通的初衷（排除 C），他单纯是在抛出自己关于语言是如何发展起来的新见解 。

句子 I believe I am the first to propose a continuity between the strong human-animal link that appeared 2.6 million years ago and the origin of language. (第7段)

Q39

解析 作者举猴子只能发出基本警告的例子，是为了引出下一句：真正的人类语言有着词汇和语法，可以无穷组合表达极其细腻的含义，从而突显人类沟通的“复杂性/高级性（sophistication）” 。

干扰 作者提猴子绝对不是为了夸猴子有语言（排除 A），而是把猴子的低级当做背景板，来反衬人类沟通能力的强大与高级 。

句子 Vervet monkeys, for example, have different cries for eagles and snakes, but they cannot discuss what threats might appear tomorrow. The property of full language is that it is comprised of vocabulary and grammatical rules that can be combined in an infinite number of ways to convey fine shades of meaning. (第7段)

Q40

解析 作者在最后一段直言不讳地说，“会走的粮仓（walking larder）”这个把动物当食物来源以解释驯化的观点，存在“根本性的缺陷（fundamental flaws）”，也就是说它未能正确解释驯化的目的 。

干扰 千万不要选 C（支持作者的观点），作者是对这个传统的粮仓理论进行无情批判的，他认为真正的原因是“熟悉度（familiarity）”而不是为了吃肉 。

句子 Domestic animals are usually considered as 'walking larders', or easy food sources, reflecting the idea that the basis of this change was a drive for greater food security. Looking at the origins of domestication for clues to its underlying reasons, I found fundamental flaws in this idea. (第8段)
